speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this being Canada's 85th birthday as a nation, I should like to suggest, supported by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and, I hope, by all hon. members, that we mark our proud and happy loyalty to our great country and to our gracious sovereign lady by rising and singing together "O Canada" and "God Save the Queen".
Whereupon the members of the house rose and sang
O Canada and
God Save the Queen.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY   APPLICATION OF GOVERNMENT TO INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION FOR DEVELOPMENT OF POWER IN INTERNATIONAL RAPIDS SECTION    EXCHANGE OF NOTES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY   APPLICATION OF GOVERNMENT TO INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION FOR DEVELOPMENT OF POWER IN INTERNATIONAL RAPIDS SECTION    EXCHANGE OF NOTES
speechtext:
I should like to table for the information of the house copies of the application of the government of Canada to the international joint commission for an order of approval of the construction of certain works for development of power in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river which I signed for the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and forwarded to the commission yesterday. I should also like to table copies of an exchange of notes
which took place at a meeting in Washington yesterday between the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), the Acting Secretary of State of the United States, Mr. Bruce, and the Canadian ambassador to the United States, Mr. Wrong. The United States government has also sent an application to the international joint commission which was signed by the Acting Secretary of State in the presence of the Minister of Transport yesterday. I am sure I am expressing the sentiments of the house when I say that we commend the Minister of Transport and the officials who have been dealing with this matter for the diligence they have shown in advancing this great project.
These applications request the international joint commission to approve the construction of works for the development of power in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river which are to be constructed by entities to be designated by the two federal governments. The works for which approval is requested are set out in section 8 of the application and are described in the agreement with the province of Ontario dated December 3, 1951, which forms the schedule to the International Rapids Power Development Act passed at the last session of parliament.
As the question of the deep waterway is not being referred to the international joint commission in the applications to which I have just referred, and as the governments of both Canada and the United States have for many years considered that navigation and power should be developed concurrently in the international rapids section, it was thought advisable to place on record, on an international basis, the nature and extent of Canada's undertaking to provide an uninterrupted waterway between lake Erie and the port of Montreal. That is the main purpose of the notes which were exchanged yesterday.
The house will recall that last September I discussed with President Truman the desirability of proceeding as quickly as possible with both the seaway and power phases of this project. We agreed that it was desirable to proceed with both phases of the project as a joint undertaking by our two countries, but I informed the President that if this were not possible, the Canadian government was prepared to proceed alone with the construction of the seaway when appropriate arrangements were made for construction of the power

St. Lawrence Power Development phases of the project. The President promised to support this alternative proposal if it was not possible to obtain congressional approval for the joint undertaking at an early date. And that having proved to be impossible, we have proceeded on this conditional undertaking that the President had given me last September.
While we shall always welcome the cooperation of the United States in undertakings of this sort which benefit the economies of both countries, it is fitting that, on the 85th anniversary of confederation, we were able to take this major step toward the accomplishment of a goal which has, for certainly at least half a century, excited the imagination of so many Canadians. And after many years of negotiations and working out of arrangements for co-operating in the joint enterprise with our great neighbour to the south, we are now prepared to construct alone this deep waterway which will link the ports of the great lakes with all the other seaports of the world.
Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the
Opposition):	In view of the fact that the
Prime Minister has expressed his hope that this announcement would meet with the approval of all hon. members, may I say without any reservation that the members of the Conservative party in the house do support this great national project as part of a general development of our resources across Canada; and in that respect I would of course wish to make it clear that there are those who naturally believe this should be a pattern of development right across Canada.
Having said that, I wish to offer my very hearty support for the indication which is given that, along with the decision to seek immediate approval of the development of the immense power resources on the St. Lawrence river, it is the decision of the Canadian government to proceed alone with the waterway development along that part of our great inland transportation system.
It is a significant thing that this announcement should be made on Dominion day when we are commemorating the birthday of Canada as a nation. This is of significance to all Canada because it is the one area where the development calls for a substantial measure of international agreement to carry forward an undertaking that we all wish to see completed as soon as possible.
Perhaps because it might have been such a striking example of international co-operation, there have been many who have expressed the hope throughout the years that the United States might see fit to join with Canada in the construction not only of
TMr. St. Laurent.)
the power development, but also of the deep waterway. This gesture between two nations which carry on their daily activities in such harmony would have been significant not only for us but for other people throughout the world who are seeking proof that nations can live in that measure of harmony and good will which we accept as a commonplace on this continent. Nevertheless, since it has been the decision, in their judgment in the United States, not to proceed with the waterway part of this development, I hope that Canada will proceed without any delay.
I wish to refer to statements that I have seen in some newspapers in the United States which convey the impression that there is still some thought in the minds of those writing editorials even in the most responsible publications that Canada is not prepared to carry on with this undertaking alone. Speaking in this house as leader of the opposition, I think it is appropriate that I should join my voice with that of the Prime Minister in expressing complete confidence that Canada is capable of proceeding alone, and that there is no doubt whatever of our ability to finance the project and also our ability to carry out the construction in a manner which will be consistent with the standards of work that have distinguished the construction of the whole of this great inland waterway system.
There are many things about which we differ, and it is the duty of the opposition to express those differences. On this occasion I wish to leave no doubt that we join in expressing the hope that this application will receive early approval, and that this whole project will proceed as an appropriate expression of Canada's confidence, on this 85th birthday, in our very great future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) have expressed the views of all hon. members. There is little to be added. I feel confident that Canada can carry this project through; and, personally, I am rather glad Canada will be undertaking the project alone. There would be some value in demonstrating co-operation between these two great countries, but on the other hand, when I look into the future, I think it is better that one of the two countries should undertake this, and be responsible for it.
I am very happy indeed that the government of Canada has decided to be the country to carry the project through. It is indeed fitting that this announcement is made on the anniversary of confederation. I want to join

in expressing appreciation of the diligence that has been shown by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and his staff, and indeed by the government, in pressing forward this great project which I believe will be, in the long run, of inestimable benefit to all of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Social Credit members have been in favour of this great project from the beginning. We, too, appreciate the fact that the announcement is being made on the 85th birthday of Canada. speechtext:
May I
ask the Prime Minister one question, by way of clarification in connection with this St. Lawrence seaway development. Assuming that Canada is proceeding with this waterway deepening alone, what constitutional difficulty could arise in virtue of the position of the United States, whereby any obstacle could be placed by the congress of the United States in the way of our proceeding alone? I ask this, having in mind what has happened before.
I can understand that, if the government has full power to approve of our going ahead on an international basis with this waterway, that would be all right; but having in mind what happened before in congress, does the Prime Minister know of any obstacle they could place in the way of Canada's developing the seaway alone?

speechtext:
Our information is that under the laws of the United States this application can be approved by the international joint commission, and that its approval under the treaty would make it binding upon the two countries. Of course the treaty could be repudiated before action is taken upon it, but I think that is most unlikely.
Secondly, according to our information the government of the United States has the right to designate the entity that would proceed with the Canadian entity in the construction of the works necessary to develop the hydroelectric power. That entity, after having been designated by the government, would have to get a licence from the federal power commission, which is a semi-judicial body. There is no action required from the congress of the United States in order to carry the project through. Of course the
St. Lawrence Power Development congress of the United States could adopt laws preventing these agencies which now exist from exercising the jurisdiction they have under the present laws. But I think that is very unlikely, also.
There is also the possibility, to which some consideration has been given, of opposing interests endeavouring to have the courts pass upon the regularity of the proceedings, and the extent of the jurisdiction of the federal power commission. That is something that would be referred to the courts. But our information from our own law officers, and from the law officers of the United States government, is that what is being done is regular, and that it is within the jurisdiction as it now exists of the federal power commission.
Of course the Canadian government cannot proceed with the seaway phase of the undertaking unless there are two entities, one Canadian and one American, that are at the same time proceeding with the power phase of the undertaking. The President had told me quite frankly that he would not favour the designation of an American entity to proceed with the power phase unless there was an undertaking to proceed concurrently with the development of the seaway. In his opinion, it was highly desirable that both phases of the project be proceeded with at the same time.
He had told me that he hoped the congress would allow the provisions of the treaty of 1941, with the appropriate amendments, to be carried out, and the two phases handled as the joint undertaking of the two countries, but that he felt it was so desirable to have the matter proceeded with at once that, if the congress did not act within a reasonable time, he would exercise his executive power to designate an agency, and to put that agency in a position where it could apply to the federal power commission for a licence.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, parliament is a great institution. Yesterday we were engaged in a most acrimonious debate which would indicate a wide separation in viewpoint; today on our national holiday parliament indicates by its action that regardless of those things that separate us in the ordinary affairs of life we stand united in the great things that make for a great Canada.
On this occasion I am going to deal for a short while as objectively as I can with the question of the redistribution of constituencies, with particular reference to what has taken place in Saskatchewan. May I say immediately that I want to thank the hon. members of all parties in the opposition who spoke yesterday so feelingly and so kindly of my constituency. In particular I want to say to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar how much I appreciate the references that he made to the nature and quality of the map drawn for the province of Saskatchewan.
Over the years I have taken the stand that committees of parliament are not very effective. Standing committees of parliament have an effective way of securing information on matters that are non-controversial and arriving at conclusions based on the greater knowledge that comes to members who participate in such committees. In the United States committees are set up under their system of government for almost every variety and type of matter that comes before congress and are generally successful in their results. I think that in large measure that is due to the fact that in the United States the members of the various political parties do not leave their independence behind when they enter congress. Over the years members of congress-it is a continuing process -consider propositions in committee regardless of any consideration that they might be negatived by the President or the party in majority in the other house. We in Canada have developed over the years the concept that after all a committee, when it is a political committee, is merely a means, either of refusal or to cover up things that are brought before it.

Generally speaking, what is taking place now has taken place in previous redistributions. In 1932 there was a long and acrimonious debate and the legislation did not pass until it had been discussed in the house for five days and then only when the prime minister had communicated with the then leader of the opposition, the Right Hon. Mr. King, and each of them appointed representatives of their respective parties to sit down and arrive at least at a basis of agreement which ended the stalemate that existed. I would have liked in this case to have the Prime Minister consider doing the same in regard to the various matters that have been brought to the attention of the house from almost every province in Canada wherein the allegation has been made, and in many cases established, that the result of the activities of the general committee was that some members were in fact subjected to gerrymandering.
I know that there are many definitions of "gerrymander", but Mr. King gave a definition which I believe reveals in its entirety the essence of the expression. Speaking in the House of Commons on May 22, 1933, as reported on page 5276 of Hansard, Mr. King said:
The word gerrymander in political parlance simply means that in redistributing a constituency the boundary lines are so altered as to do an obvious injury to one political party and give an obvious unfair political advantage to another party.
That was the definition that he gave at that time. He pointed out on that occasion the difficulty, or the impossibility even, of a committee composed of representative members of the House of Commons, having regard to the emotions that are aroused and the considerations that appeal to each and every individual, being able to arrive at fairness in connection with the redistribution of seats that might take place. Today we find ourselves too often in the position where our committee system becomes merely a means whereby a rubber stamping of government policy is carried out by the ciphers appointed to that committee. In every case the decision is dominated by government majority. No one is suggesting that the government should not have the majority on a committee, but certainly no one can suggest that anything approaching judicial or judicious consideration is given to the determination of the conclusions arrived at by committees.
I am going to refer for a moment in general to what the evidence yesterday disclosed. Summarized, it indicated that there had been a gerrymander and that the decision arrived at in a number of cases, in particular those affecting opposition members, had been prejudiced as well as prejudged. Sufficient was

said yesterday and in recent weeks to indicate that a gerrymander has been effected by arriving at constituency boundaries in a manner that indicates that considerations other than symmetry were involved; in other cases by the dissimilarity in population and in still other cases by joinders that were made of opposition constituencies.
I am going to refer for a moment to what was said yesterday by the hon. member for Melfort, who dealt with the Saskatchewan situation. I am going to review what took place in determining the recommendations made by the subcommittee. The hon. member referred to the constituency of Melfort where a grotesque result was produced for political purposes. When the hon. member made a motion in the committee that an alteration should be made in the constituency of Mel-fort-Humboldt in order to remove a line of townships that had no place in any fair constituency map, after a discussion lasting a matter of two or three minutes, in came the hon. member for St. Boniface to act as chairman of the committee. The vote was three to three and he cast a vote in favour of a refusal to accept the suggestion made by the hon. member for Melfort. When I point out what took place in the Saskatchewan committee I do so because of the fact that it places before the house something of the activity or lack of activity that was apparent in the committee. The committee met for one or two minutes prior to the Saskatchewan general election. On that occasion I asked for the production of the map because there had been maps in the press that bore a peculiarly prophetic appearance in the light of the final map as it actually was. I asked whether or not there was a map and the members, including the chairman, said there was not. If there was not, then all I can say is that the prospective projection that appeared in the press bore such a similarity to the final result as to indicate at least some foreknowledge on the part of the press as to the composition of the map.
I said if it were not produced before the election I would certainly take it for granted that the prospective map published by the press indicating what was going to be done did in fact indicate what was to be done. By agreement there were no more meetings until after the election. Following the election certain meetings were held to which the hon. member for Kamloops has alluded. He has revealed what took place and has also indicated that the length of time taken did not exceed a few minutes and that there was no discussion regarding what should or should not be done. Proceeding a bit further, on June 23 there was a meeting. That was the
Redistribution
one to which the hon. member for Kamloops made reference yesterday. He asked for the production of the map on the Friday preceding the 23rd of June and was advised that there was no map. On the 23rd of June we met and the map was produced. We looked it over. There was about twenty minutes' discussion and there was only one copy of the map there. We asked for copies of the map and were advised there were none available. A little later the hon. member for Rosthern said that copies would be made available, and at five o'clock that afternoon I received one. It was understood that the subcommittee would meet again later that day, but the hon. member for Rosthern agreed that it should not meet until the next day.
On June 24 we met for a total period of not over half an hour. The map was produced. The attitude taken was: There is your map; that is all there is to it. There was no question of compromise, no question of discussion and no question of the consideration of the wishes of any member of the committee except those who produced the map as an accomplished fact. On that occasion the hon. member for Melfort made a motion, and I have already told the committee the result of that motion. I also pointed out that there was something obviously wrong with the Prince Albert constituency with respect to the removal of an area in the southeastern corner thereof extending from Kilwinning to Blaine Lake, an area of approximately twenty-four miles square and one which has been in Prince Albert constituency throughout the years. No explanation was given.
Following that I made certain motions. I moved that certain changes be made, and in particular that the area in the western part of the constituency of Lake Centre, which has been in that constituency ever since Lake Centre was created, the area extending from Hawarden to Elbow and along the South Saskatchewan river from Kenaston to Aylesbury, including the towns of Craik and Davidson, should continue to be within the constituency. I also referred to the fact that the populations of Melville and Qu'Appelle constituencies did not nearly approximate that of Lake Centre. There was no discussion of the matter at all. The hon. member for St. Boniface was there. A vote was taken the result of which was three for and three against, and the deciding vote was cast by the hon. member for St. Boniface.
On the evening of June 24 the matter came before the general committee. In other words the matter had not been before the subcommittee for a total period of over one hour. There was no question of any discussion. There was nothing but the applied steamroller. The general committee met and

Redistribution
the chairman and other members of the general committee asked on that occasion that the subcommittee should sit again the next day for the purpose of discussing the question. In pursuance of what the general committee had decided, the subcommittee met on June 25 at ten o'clock in the morning in the room of the hon. member for Rosthern to reconsider the matter as requested by the general committee. As soon as we were convened the question was asked whether or not there was any change, and the hon. member for Rosthern said "no". An inquiry was made whether they had any suggestions to offer and the answer was "No, this is the map." We met for two minutes. That was the total discussion that took place at any time and the complete consideration given in determining the revamping and redrafting of constituencies in Saskatchewan. I ask you, Mr. Chairman: Is that the consideration that members of the opposition deserve? Certainly we did not expect to get some of the things that we wanted but at least we should not have had a map placed before us as certain in its effect as the law of the Medes and the Persians, and as certainly subject to no appeal or consideration.
I have mentioned the fact that for a considerable period of time it had been said that tremendous changes would be made in the constituency of Lake Centre. Mention was made yesterday of populations. I do not recall the minister saying that. I have Hansard here and I will look at it. If the minister said that, then there is no question about it but I did not get that in my notes. I will look at Hansard to see just how fully the minister did say it.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I give you this picture and I simply point out that after all no one asks for consideration other than justice. No consideration but justice. One does not ask to be discriminated in favour of, but every member of this house has the right to ask that he be not discriminated against. And I ask you this, Mr. Chairman: Viewing the matter as reasonably as possible how can anyone justify taking the constituency boundaries in this way and removing from the west side of that constituency an area most heavily populated within the constituency? They remove there a large number of townships of which I will give the exact detail- and a township is six miles square. That area has always been in Lake Centre. It was in the constituency that was the predecessor of Lake Centre-west of the lake-

the old Long Lake constituency. They remove that area and it is merely a coincidence that the constituency represents an area wherein, as Mr. King said in 1932, a large majority is to be found for a Conservative candidate. Then, the city of Moose Jaw is added to this constituency-a city of
24,000	or 25,000 population, and a city that is growing. I have no objection to that because changes must take place and I want to be fair, but I cannot understand any justification for a city being placed in a rural constituency. Trying to be fair you can say: All right, after all changes take place; and I offer no other conjecture but that it is coincidence that two opposition members are thus covered by the joinder.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I point out this fact. Here is the Qu'Appelle constituency represented by the hon. member who was one of those who participated in the modern Mercator's projection and apparently he objected to the area around Regina. At no time was the area surrounding Regina ever in Lake Centre, as the minister said yesterday. The only area that was ever in Lake Centre was the area west of Regina, and the word "surround" to me does not imply surrounding on one side. You made no qualifications yesterday. It is the same old thing. Yesterday the statement was "surrounding" and there can be no "surrounding" of a city or of any other place by merely being adjacent to one boundary line.
There was one change made to the map in the committee. At the last meeting of the committee the hon. member for Rosthern I believe asked if there were any changes; and he himself answered his own question and said in effect that we are going to add three miles across the entire southern boundary of the constituency of Qu'Appelle, and that was passed. That raises the population from 40,650, as originally intended, to 43,300; but the area east of Regina has been in Qu'Appelle for years. No objection was raised in 1947.
Redistribution
It is now being tacked on to the constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. If they really want to preserve names they also should have Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and Regina city junior; for after all, it takes from Regina city, and out of the confines of Regina city, several thousands of population. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, is that justice? Is that fairness? Somebody may say, as does the Canadian Press today, "Oh well, an alteration was made yesterday." The effect of the alteration yesterday was simply to add one column of townships on the east boundary line wherein the population is almost equally divided politically, except for this area around Regina which is within Regina city and which is still to be put into a constituency of Lake Centre-Moose Jaw city. Can there be any justification for adding approximately 5,000 city population from Regina-right out of the incorporated city-besides the several hundreds if not thousands who live in the suburbs of Regina, all of whom will now be placed in Lake Centre although not within the incorporated portion of the city of Regina?
Mr. Chairman, the object of representation by population is to assure equality. The changes that are made are made only because it is more difficult to represent a large area in a rural constituency than it is to represent a city; and there are other physical features that demand changes. But let any hon. member view this picture and ask himself whether that fairness and impartiality that is expected is exhibited by those who place in a rural constituency, which is still a matter of about sixty miles wide and eighty miles in length, one city and, not satisfied with that, place in it 5,000 population from another city, forty miles removed from the first.
Mr. Chairman, I repeat what I said a while ago. No one asks for favours; but on behalf of the people I represent in that western part of that constituency and also on behalf of the people in Regina and in Moose Jaw I ask that there should be no discrimination against them any more than there should be personal discrimination against any member of the house.
It is said that the name remains. The other day there was an interruption by the hon. member for Rosthern who said, "It still has the name." Let us see what about the area. There were 192 townships in Lake Centre and the population was approximately that of the adjoining constituencies. It was not large. I think the population was some 35,000. But there were five smaller populations than that in the province in these areas. People have moved away. That is why we have been asking

It was for that reason that the chairman of the subcommittee for Saskatchewan made the remarks he did a few moments ago. The details of the discussions that took place were known only to members of the committee. The chairman has recited what did take place in the committee and therefore I am not going to discuss that further.
There are some peculiarities about the Saskatchewan situation which are unique to that province. In the first place, we were not entitled under the constitution as it existed to 17 members; we were entitled to 15 only. After listening to the discussion, particularly by the two hon. members who were most concerned, I have been wondering whether we improved the situation by increasing the number to 17.
Before saying anything more about it I want to thank hon. members from all parts of Canada and from all sides of the house for listening to the representations that were made by the Prime Minister to the effect that some change should be made because one province was being asked to drop 25 per cent of its membership in the house under the constitution as it then was. At the time that suggestion was made, if it was not suggested in so many words it was certainly inferred that it would be impossible to make what would be looked upon in this country as a reasonable adjustment of the seats if an attempt was made to take 5 seats out of the 20 in the province of Saskatchewan. It was agreed unanimously that there should be 17 seats.
Whether we were right or whether we were wrong, we took it for granted that when that decision was made there were at least two members from Saskatchewan to whom some consideration had to be given. One was the leader of the C.C.F. party who has a seat in that province-the leaders of other parties have seats in other provinces-and the other was the hon. member for Lake Centre. Neither of them seems to have appreciated that we did anything for him at all. That was the central fact in connection with redistribution in Saskatchewan to which the members of the Saskatchewan subcommittee had to pay attention.
It would have been a simple matter to have redistributed the seats in Saskatchewan and have them all within one thousand of one

another in population, if we were not required to pay any attention to that fact. The areas in which there is a shortage of population are apparent to everyone. If you take the west side of Saskatchewan and divide it into constituencies as it is now, you find that under the census of 1951 Kindersley had 34,325; Maple Creek had 32,500; Meadow Lake had 35,511; Swift Current with a city had 42,600. The Battlefords with a city had 44,382 and Rosetown-Biggar had 33,033.
If one were to remove the cities from that group he would have four rural seats in that area which would only have had an average population of less than 40,000. Therefore it was obvious that one constituency should come out. The easiest constituency to have taken out was Rosetown-Biggar. I think even the hon. member will agree that the simplest thing to have done was to have taken out the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar and run one constituency east and west instead of north and south. We would then have had a rate of population for the constituencies which would have thrown the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in along with the hor.. member for Kindersley. They would have had to contest that constituency. I can imagine what would have been said if we had done that, but that was the simplest and easiest thing to do.
What did we do? We took a Liberal seat out of that area, just removed it. We did not remove any C.C.F. seats. We did not remove any Conservative seats. We removed a Liberal seat from that area, and when I say "we" I mean our committee from the province of Saskatchewan. Those who were on that committee representing the Liberals made that recommendation. There has been a lot of discussion about when there was a map and when there was not a map. These other matters were the important questions to be discussed in the first instance. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says that if the matter had been referred to a commission there would have been quite a different map. I agree that there would have been, and his seat would not have been in it.
There would have been no constituency of Rosetown-Biggar running down south of the river. There could not have been enough population obtained to put a seat there at all unless it did run south of the river because of the very situation outlined a few moments ago by the hon. member for Lake Centre, namely, that is a part of the province that is going down in population and going down very rapidly. Because it is a part of the province that is going down very rapidly and because of the fact that two additional seats had been put into Saskatchewan largely because of the difficulty that would have been

involved in trying to make an adjustment of 25 per cent in population with relation to the population in other provinces in any one redistribution, we were given special consideration. I think we treated that special consideration in the manner in which it was intended to be treated by leaving the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar there with the result that the leader of that party does not have to contest the seat with any other member of the house.
That was the first consideration and the committee acted upon it. If anyone wants to know what the opinion of the Saskatchewan caucus was on that question, that was their opinion. The committee of three appointed by that caucus was definitely instructed that there had to be a seat of Rosetown-Biggar when the map was drawn no matter how it was drawn, and that it had to remain there because of the special consideration we had been given.
Coming now to Lake Centre, I quite agree that Lake Centre has been a matter of controversy ever since the hon. member for Lake Centre came into this house. I quite agree too that he is quite capable of expressing his point of view on any question on which he has a mind to express it. A further fact is that the northeastern section of it was treed before the white man came, and as the white man has cleared the trees off that part it is just as level as the other section. That is different, and when someone across the floor yesterday was saying there were only so few people someone said, "Well, there are a lot of rocks there," and the suggestion was made that maybe they ought to count the rocks. Well, our province is different. You can go into our province and you can draw squares or oblongs all over the province and get pretty nearly the kind of result in one area that you get in any other, but that is more difficult in other provinces.
I agree with the member for Melfort that when the map was drawn five years ago those squares were made just about as they ought to be and the population in them was comparatively equal. Now we are asked: Why is it a little different this time? Again, I agree that if anyone has reason for complaint it is the people who live in the northeastern section of the province. Those constituencies are higher than average.
That brings me back to the question now being discussed a few minutes ago as to what I said yesterday. I do not need to read it but I have turned it up and it is there. I

know what I said yesterday and on some other days as well in spite of what some members may think. Yesterday I did not refer to the fact that we had under consideration these two seats of Rosetown-Biggar and of Lake Centre as being fundamental in drawing any map; but I did refer to the remainder, namely that the first thing we had to agree on was that there should be two city seats-Regina and Saskatoon-irrespective of what the population happened to be. When you take those out that gets your population down to a certain level. Then I said the next thing we considered was that there were six other seats-with smaller cities in them. We suggested that when the committee was drawing a map they should allow those constituencies about 50,000 each. That is 300,000 in the six. We deducted that from the total population. That left us nine rural constituencies without any city population in them at all and we divided nine into the remainder of the population.
That gave us a unit and the unit is between
44,000	and 45,000 for the rural seats. The only criticism I have heard with regard to the constituencies is that people start out by saying: Look at the seat of the Minister of Agriculture. Well, the seat of the Minister of Agriculture has 43,300 in it, which is within 1,000 of the unit. That applies in any seat. I then wish to say this about that seat. I have not always represented it in this house. It has been there ever since the province of Saskatchewan was set up and it has had almost its present boundary lines during all that time. When you look at that constituency today and compare it with the rest of Canada you will see it is within 1,000 of the population to which it is entitled under any redistribution. Consider it in relation to all the other constituencies in Canada-and after all that is what we were getting down to when we made a redistribution.

I mean that when you take the city seats out of Saskatchewan, and no one questions two of them should have members of their own, and when you take out the six smaller city seats with 50,000 each, I think everyone will agree that your representation is reasonably fair when the unit turns out to be 44,500 for these purely rural seats, or about there. There is not very much complaint then. Our rural seats are only 5,000 below our city seats and our smaller city seats are only 5,000 or 6,000 below our larger city seats, so there is not very much for anyone to complain about. If you once agree to that as the proper unit

for the rural seats in Saskatchewan as compared with all the remainder of Canada, we are comparable with the rural seats elsewhere. They can be made more nearly exact in our province because of what I said-by the very nature of the province. Ours is an agricultural province largely settled by the same kind of people in the same kind of areas. You can make them about the same size and you can make them about the same in population. That was our intention in 1947 and it was our intention again here.
That intention was affected somewhat by this other point I raised a few moments ago, namely that we have to make provision for these two constituencies and do not forget that we had to take out three seats. We took out one down in the southwest because there was not enough population up across the west side to keep our unit up close to 44,000 in the rural areas and at the same time keep our two city seats in that district up to about
50,000.	So we wound up with 50,000 in the Swift Current seat, and we wound up with
48.000	in the Battleford seat and around
44.000	in the others except in the extreme north seat which has only 35,000. I think it will be agreed for the extreme north seat stretching almost over to the Manitoba boundary that there is justification for having
35.000	there, and the others are just about as they should be according to the adjustment that was made.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee adjourned for lunch, I was dealing with the eastern side of Saskatchewan and more particularly with my own constituency. I had pointed out to the committee that we in Saskatchewan were working under special conditions, one of them being that we were given two constituencies in addition to those that we were entitled to under the constitution as it had previously been drawn and which required of us some things which I had discussed.
Then I had pointed out that the western side of the province was the part that had been reduced in population-and considerably reduced-in the ten-year period with the result that one constituency had to be taken out of the west side. I had also pointed out that the constituency which was taken out by the committee was a seat which is now represented in the House of Commons by a Liberal. If we had simply had the intention of doing what has been suggested from the other side of the house has been the main objective of Liberals, I think we could have found a way of taking out a seat other than one of the Liberal seats.
Then I had undertaken to give a similar review of the eastern side of the province and had started with my own constituency, the reason being that most of those who have been discussing the question of redistribution as related to Saskatchewan have referred to the fact that the population in my constituency is 43,500. I had pointed out that that figure is within 1,000 of the normal, average population for a rural constituency in Saskatchewan.
Just before the committee adjourned I had made the remark that the constituency which I represent in the House of Commons has not changed much since the province of Saskatchewan was first formed. The boundary lines of the seat are almost exactly the same on the south. They are the same as far as they go on the east side. They are almost identical on the north side. They end, or did end prior to what we did yesterday, at the same place on the west end. Hence, over the period of years there has not been much change.
The only effective change was along the east side where prior to the time that I was in politics at all, either provincially or federally, the constituency ran northward along the Manitoba boundary up to Togo or up to the Assiniboine river, then followed the Assiniboine river for a way, then ran west and down on the east side of Yorkton.

Redistribution
In other words, it cut Yorkton out of the seat but took in that section between Yorkton and Manitoba. If we had simply been trying to strengthen the constituency at this time, I would say that we would have put that section back on again because it is a Liberal section and one in which I am satisfied that I could get at least two-thirds of the votes. But we did not do that. We left the boundaries much as they were and we left the population within
1,000	of the average for rural constituencies in the province of Saskatchewan.
Because of the method by which that procedure was worked out, and which I outlined just before lunch, it places that constituency in the position where it bears the proper relationship to populations right across Canada and it bears out the statement that that constituency is at least one constituency in Canada which, since 1914, has continued to bear the same relationship to the population of all the rest of Canada as it did in 1914. In other words, the development of that section of the province has been on a par with the development in other sections of the Dominion of Canada. I am sorry that is not true of the whole province of Saskatchewan but it is true of that particular area and [DOT] that particular constituency.
Then the seat immediately north of it is Yorkton; and under the plan which has been submitted to the house, that constituency will have a population of 50,000. That is exactly the population which it was calculated at the beginning that it should have, because that is a constituency with a city, one of the smaller cities of Saskatchewan. Yorkton is a city and Yorkton constituency will have a population of approximately 50,000 under this arrangement. That really cut off the north from the south. There are two seats in that area running east and west from the Manitoba boundary to the boundary of Lake Centre. These two constituencies having within themselves all the requirements for units make a cut-off as between the Qu'Appelle river and the north. In view of the fact that I represent part of that area it was suggested to me that I draw a map. I do not know what suggestion was made to other members; there has been some dispute here this morning as to whether it was suggested that some members draw a map, but all I wish to say about it is that there was nothing to prevent anybody from drawing a map. Anyone who was on any one of these committees could have drawn maps to his heart's content and could have submitted them to the committees and had them considered. There never was anything to prevent anyone from doing that.

I drew a map with regard to my own area. As the basis of that map I took the redistribution that was submitted to the house by the Tories in 1933. I quite agree the map of 1933 did not go through the house. Nevertheless, the map was submitted. I obtained one of the maps and found what were the boundaries; not that were passed by the house but that were submitted to the house. The constituency as suggested at that time was a constituency of Yorkton-Melville running north and south; not a constituency running east and west, but one running north and south. If you take the boundary line of that constituency as it was suggested at that time and put both the town of Melville and the city of Yorkton into the same constituency you have a population of just about 50,000, taking in the proposed area. Therefore it could have been justified to have drawn it in that way.
Well, my suggestion to our own people was: why not draw it that way? And then we took a look at the next constituency alongside of it. If you put another constituency running north and south, with the present populations, starting at the Qu'Appelle valley and running it right over to Long lake, you would have had to go away up into the constituency of Humboldt in order to get enough population to make it a constituency. In other words, you would have wiped out half of the constituency of Lake Centre, and so naturally our people said at once: if you are going to carry out the undertaking which the caucus decided in the first place was a reasonable undertaking, that cannot be done. You cannot take and put another constituency in there and run it up north and take off the whole east half of the constituency of Lake Centre. That is the reason why the decision was reached that they would not do that, they would not take out two old constituencies and substitute two running north and south. What relation has that got to the fact that there are 42,000 or 43,000 people in Qu'Appelle south of the Qu'Appelle river, and that there are about 42,000 in Assiniboia, down in the southeast corner?

speechtext: Moose Mountain.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

Yes; it used to be Assiniboia. The relationship is this. There is only one way that you could increase that population in Moose Mountain, and that was to extend the constituency westward. You have to extend it westward only six miles until you take the city of Weyburn into it. The city of Weyburn is the centre of population of the constituency of Assiniboia, which is represented in this house by a C.C.F. member. Well, we could have increased the population of Qu'Appelle and the population of Assiniboia

or of Moose Mountain up to something approaching 50,000 by that one movement. But by that one movement we would have to cut off a very considerable part of the constituency of Assiniboia. As a matter of fact, if we had proceeded on that basis, we would have to cut out the constituency of Assiniboia altogether.
We did not think that was a reasonable thing to do, and we therefore had to consider something else. The something else resulted in the fact that by leaving Weyburn in Assiniboia, by leaving a constituency in the southeast corner at around 42,000, which is about 2,000 below the average for that province, we could still continue Assiniboia in the province, provided we had one thing, provided that we did not go far enough to take Moose Jaw in. If we went far enough to take Moose Jaw in, then we had to start all over again on the whole adjustment of populations in order to meet the situation. But by taking Weyburn, and the area up to within six miles or ten miles of Moose Jaw, in the constituency of Assiniboia we had a population of somewhere between 48,000 and 50,000 people: in other words, the population which was required in order to meet the condition that we have 50,000 in constituencies where there are small cities was satisfied.
We had Weyburn within that constituency. That, too, removed another complication. If we had done it in any other way, and provided for a constituency in the south central part of the province of Saskatchewan, we would have to go far enough north to take in Moose Jaw. If we had done that we would have been accused immediately of wiping out a C.C.F. seat. It is all very well to be accused of putting the hon. member for Lake Centre and the hon. member for Moose Jaw in the same constituency, but to have put the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Moose Jaw in the same constituency would have meant wiping out one of those members, and saying that he had no constituency in which one or other could run. Well, I can imagine what would have been said in the house if we had done that.

I have pointed out to you that we could move only as we did move around from the southeast corner until we got up to Moose Jaw; we could not move the boundary line

of Yorkton to take in population, and therefore we left the line just about where it was.
This all brings me into the northern seats that the hon. member for Melfort has said have too much population. I agree with him that if there was nothing else to be considered, and nothing else that should have been considered, his criticism is a reasonable and legitimate one. There are 48,000 people in the constituency of Mackenzie. There are about 52,000 people in the constituency of Humboldt-Melfort as it is drafted.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: There are 49,600 in Mackenzie, and 53,500 in Humboldt-Melfort.

There are over 50,000 in one, and over 48,000 in the other. When you get the figures adjusted I think you will find they are just about as stated. But anyway, it is within reasonable distance of the 50,000 in the one case. Then, when you go over to the constituency of Rosthern it is 48,000. There are still a few to be added to that. Then when you get into Prince Albert it is
56,000	and a few. I quite agree that these constituencies of Prince Albert, Rosthern, Humboldt-Melfort and Mackenzie are higher than they would be if you could adjust the whole thing to meet the situation exactly over the whole province; and they are perhaps high on an average by about 2,000 or 3,000 per constituency.
Well, we examined into every possible way of adjusting them differently from what they are without interfering with the other things I have spoken of. We had to take three members out. We had taken one Liberal in the south. We had to start somewhere in the centre in order to get rid of two more. And we tried to do it without, with our pencils, driving people out of this house. There was only one way of being able to do that without driving people out of this house, and that was to have at least two constituencies in which members would have the right to refer the matter to the people in the area rather than for a committee of this house to sit down and draw a line around a particular area and say: This person is out; he has no convention to go to. We did not do it in that way. We looked the whole area over and proposed to the house what has been proposed.
In so far as Humboldt-Melfort is concerned, I understand that, apart from saying the population is a little high, the hon. member had only one proposal to make, namely, that four townships up in the northeast corner of the constituency be moved out of his seat over into the other. It has been suggested

Redistribution
that it is in the constituency only because of one reason. It is in the constituency only because when the line was being drawn and came up to a certain point it came head on into a railroad, and all of the railroad south of there is in the constituency of Mackenzie. Then, if you drew the line straight on north, !it would cut across that railroad again about ten miles farther north, and it would cut out two towns, New Osgoode and one other over into the constituency of Humboldt-Melfort, and leave the territory which is tributary to those towns over in the constituency of Mackenzie.
Well, all that was done on that map was to run a line across six miles of the southern boundary of the township, and run it 24 miles north to give the boundary of the other constituency. And that not only put the whole railway with all the towns on the railway into the one constituency, and all the territory tributary to the towns into the one constituency, but when you go up to the north end there is another railway which comes to an end in the corner of that constituency just over the boundary line. And instead of leaving the spur sticking out there, a spur that had no relation to any other area, that spur is also still in the constituency of Humboldt-Melfort.
Now, that is the only reason it is there, and I think it is a good reason. I repeat that the only amendment I know of that was moved by the hon. member, who is a member of the committee, was that those four townships be put over into the other seat. I do not know that there is any very good reason for doing it. I still think it would be a bad thing for people in that area, no matter how they are going to vote or whom they are going to vote for, to be put in a position where they are not properly related to the railways and towns in the area where they live.
I do not know whether that reason satisfies those who think the population up in the north is greater in those constituencies than it should be. But it is the only way that was found for adjusting the position in relation to what we must do down south. It provided a seat in which two members now in the house may run.
That brings me back to the constituency of Lake Centre. We have a number of constituencies right up through the central part of the province on the map as it is now drawn. They were Assiniboia, with 39,917 people in it before the new map was drawn; Moose Jaw, the third largest city in Saskatchewan, with only 42,000 people in it. I will read the round figures. Then we had Lake Centre with 36,000 in it. Then we had
IMr. Gardiner.]
Rosthern with 34,000 in it. Then we had Regina with 66,000.
Now, that is Regina as it was under the census of 1941, and as it is on the map now as a constituency-66,000. Then we had the old constituency of Saskatoon with 58,000. But that constituency had considerable rural area in it. Then there is Prince Albert with 46,936.
One has only to read those figures in order to realize that, apart from Regina and Saskatoon, every constituency in that area is away below its unit of population-every constituency. There was not any way of taking Regina out. There was not any way of ignoring the fact that Saskatoon was there. And so what was done was to take the population in the constituency of Regina, as it was before, and the population in the constituency of Saskatoon, as it is anticipated in the present schedule, add them together and subtract that from the population of Saskatchewan, as I indicated, in order to take the first step in making the adjustment. Then the next step was to take the six city seats and adjust them up to around 50,000.
Now, Moose Jaw was one of those city seats-the largest city, apart from Regina and Saskatoon. Prince Albert is another. It is the fourth largest city-much larger than any of the other smaller cities. And so I think it would have been fair under any circumstances to have had Prince Albert a little above the 50,000. But I still admit that
56.000	is pretty high for Prince Albert. And I still admit that some of the other constituencies-for example, let us take The Battlefords with 48,000-are a little low. When you compare The Battlefords with Moose Jaw, the population of Moose Jaw being 53,000 and that of The Battlefords
48.000,	that is the position it results in, an adjustment of city and rural seats. Averaging the two you are not far away from what we are driving at when we try to make an adjustment which will be satisfactory.
Now, coming back to the situation so far as Lake Centre is concerned:	There were
not very many people left, no matter how you looked at it, to provide for one rural constituency. The best you could find is
20.000	people; and if you were going to leave Rosetown-Biggar with the 44,500, which is the average, and if you were going to leave the two constituencies on the east side, one with 43,500 and the other with approximately
50.000,	then there were only 20,000 rural people in the area that was left in Lake Centre. There was only one way of getting sufficient population to take care of a situation of that kind, and that was to take some of the city population along with the rural area.

There are 26,000 people in Moose Jaw. That
26,000	plus 20,000 would have been only
46,000,	with the third largest city in the province in the constituency. The northern part of the city of Regina outside the city limits, as they were in 1941, had already been in Moose Jaw, over to the main road that comes in from the north. The other small corner of the city on the east side had been, since 1933, in the constituency of Qu'Appelle.
That seems to be the one question which has been uppermost in the minds of hon. members of the committee. They say: Why could that not have been left in Regina? There are several reasons, the first of which is the fact that it was not in Regina before. Then there is the further fact that population had to be found in order to have a constituency in that area with a reasonable population. If you were going to have city population in it, 30,000 city people plus 20,000 rural people is not a bad combination in a province such as Saskatchewan.
With all due respect to those who have been discussing the question, I would point this out, that there is not a single person in any of the groups on the other side of the house who has said that the committee, either acting as three from the Liberal side of the house or acting with three from the other side of the house, has tried to gerrymander those two seats so that Liberals could win. There is no one who has suggested that the Liberal party could win Rosetown-Biggar. There is no one who has even suggested that a Liberal could win Moose Jaw-Lake Centre-and I am not suggesting they could either.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Who will, then?

I will try to get the Liberals to win, if possible; but I am not saying that they can win, any more than hon. members on the other side of the house have been saying it. As a matter of fact Saskatchewan is in some respects a peculiar province. We have always been voting Liberal up until quite recently. We still voted almost as strongly Liberal three or four weeks ago as we ever voted in our history. Still we did not elect as many people as we thought we might.
There is another peculiarity about Saskatchewan, and this will be confirmed by the records. We never did have a Liberal representing Rosetown-Biggar in this house, either as it is constituted at the present time or as it was constituted when it was called Saskatoon county. It was represented by John Evans for some years, and when it was taken away from Mr. Evans it was taken by a Conservative, Mr. Loucks. It is the strongest
Redistribution
Conservative section in the province of Saskatchewan; there is no question about that. It has been represented by Conservatives in the local house; it has been represented by Conservatives in the federal house; it has never been represented by Liberals in the federal house.
Then coming to the constituency that has been known as Lake Centre. The Conservatives set it up in its present form, but before that Long lake was on the west side of Long Lake constituency and it was represented in this house by Dr. Cowan.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: One parliament, that is all.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Yes, represented by Dr. Cowan for one parliament. Peculiarly that was one parliament during which the Conservatives were winning across the Dominion of Canada. It was not considered a bad thing to have eight members from the province of Saskatchewan when they were winning across Canada. They had one out of Long Lake; they had one out of what is now Rosetown-Biggar; they had one out of Saskatoon; they had one out of Moose Jaw and they had one out of Melfort. That is, from a district running angleways down from the north into that central group of constituencies, practically all these seats coming within that group, are seats right in the middle of Saskatchewan-I should have said they had one from Regina, one from Qu'Appelle, and one from Battle-ford, which is angling out in two other directions. In other words, if there is any Tory stronghold in Saskatchewan, that is it, centring right around Outlook and from there east and west.
There were a great many reasons for that. I am not going to recite them here because I do not want to give information to the Tory party. As I say, there were a lot of reasons as to why it was that way. All one has to do is to examine the records to find out that what I am stating is correct.
There is another thing to consider. The province of Saskatchewan has voted on a few occasions. In 1929 we had 170,000 Liberal votes in Saskatchewan, and there were
134,000	Conservative votes. That was the vote for the Conservative party under the leadership of Dr. Anderson as late as 1929. That is about the way the province of Saskatchewan had divided itself in politics from the time it was formed in 1905 down to that period. The only reason why we were defeated on that occasion was that the Independents and Progressives joined with the Conservatives and afterwards formed a coalition government.

There was a Conservative vote of 117,000 at that time. The hon. member for Rosthern said this morning that if all the Conservatives that voted in the last provincial election had voted in one constituency they would not elect a Conservative. In other words, there were about 8,000 of them. Of course one can take these figures from Hansard and put them together in different ways and reach different conclusions; but one conclusion will be that there were not very many Conservatives who had a chance to vote in the last election. If they had had a chance to vote the results would have been quite different in a number of constituencies and we would be in a better position today to be quoting majorities.
The hon. member for Lake Centre has been quoting the votes in different polls in the recent election in the province of Saskatchewan. I agree with him that they do not mean much in certain areas. It is still possible to elect Conservatives in the province of Saskatchewan despite what some people think, but there are certain ways of doing it and certain ways of seeing that it is not done. I do not know of anyone who is working to see that it is not done except the Conservatives themselves in the way they are not keeping their organization alive and not nominating candidates when elections come around. How in the world can anybody vote Conservative when he has not a candidate to vote for? If you have no candidate to vote for you just cannot vote at all. You can vote without a leader, but not without a candidate.
That has been the situation and I do not think it is going to help by quoting votes in different polls under the circumstances that have existed during the last two or three elections. I should like to direct attention to the fact that in our last vote we were not very far from the peak vote we had in Saskatchewan of 206,000. Therefore we are back pretty nearly to where we were in 1929 when there was an arrangement made under which the opposition did

not run any two candidates against one another and in which they finished on top.
If I was looking for an opportunity to advise our friends of the Conservative party I would call their attention to their own representations. No one on the other side of the house has said one word about the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar, which is a Conservative constituency, being so organized as to favour a Liberal. No one has raised the question as to whether we were trying to take the Lake Centre constituency away from the member for Lake Centre. It is obvious to the member for Lake Centre, it is obvious to the C.C.F., it is obvious to everyone else that if we had been trying to do that we would have done something very different from what is indicated on this map.

The vote in that constituency is naturally a Conservative vote, and there are reasons for that which do not need to be explained. All I am suggesting is we have not done anything to try to take a seat away from somebody. We have simply said that we have got to get rid of three members somehow because we have three fewer seats. We have got twenty members now and there can only be seventeen seats. We said we were not going to draw a line around any seat except that of one Liberal. We took away the Liberal seat but we said we were not going to draw a line around any other seat and take it away from either a C.C.F.'er or a Conservative. We said that we would recommend the lines to be drawn in such a way that the people in the constituencies could settle the matter. I do not know what my C.C.F. friends have in mind to do with some of their candidates. I only know that on occasions gone by they have read some of them out of the party. I hope they are not going to do that on this occasion because we did not read any of them out of their party or out of this house.
I am quite satisfied to accept the statements made across the floor of the house that

there are two good men in the constituencies of Moose Jaw and Lake Centre who now represent those seats in the house, and I would not be at all surprised if either one or the other could be elected in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. I would not be at all surprised either if one of them went home and could be elected elsewhere. But when a member comes down into the middle of the strongest Tory section in Saskatchewan and wishes to take all the Tories into his constituency so he can be sure of being elected, I say to him if that is what the Conservative party wants they are decidedly on their way out.

You have got to examine a little further in order to find out who was elected and who was not. A Liberal was not elected in a great number of instances because of an arrangement entered into. But now that I am questioned about it I do want to say that the first time I ever met my hon. friend was at a meeting right in the area he has been talking about today. I Spoke at Elbow in 1928 and my hon. friend turned up and asked for the right to speak at the same meeting. I had never seen him before although I had heard of him because he used to be a Liberal. I had heard of him as the secretary of the Liberal party in a certain place. But on this occasion in 1928 he turned up, and I am not going into details as to what the 1928 election meant in the constituency of Arm River. I am going to suggest, however, that was my first experience in meeting him. I campaigned every poll in that constituency on that occasion. I canvassed most of the people and we succeeded in winning the election by fifty-eight votes. If anybody wants to tell me that is not a Conservative seat let me say that I 55704-256

know Saskatchewan well enough to know that it is.
I know Saskatchewan well enough to be able to say that I think very fair treatment has been accorded to the Conservatives in the province in so far as the drafting of the new constituencies is concerned. We have not attempted to make any change in the two seats which we were under obligation, as I said at the beginning, to draw up in such a way as to give consideration to two members. We were given two extra seats and we were expected to deal with them fairly. We think we did. So far as the other seats are concerned, not a single member has asked for any change in his own seat except the hon. member for Melfort and he only asked that four townships be moved into another constituency. I doubt if there is any other province in Canada where as good a job has been done, and I rather resent people getting up and saying that the committee made a miserable job of it or that they did something which was detrimental to some person, group or party. We do not think they did any such thing, and I am quite satisfied that if anyone will sit down and examine the map of Saskatchewan, and take into consideration the facts as I have outlined them, they will agree that the presentation of the province of Saskatchewan to this committee is just as good as has been made by any other province, and in addition it is just as good as could have been made by any kind of commission that you might appoint.
I want to add one other thing. I have been in politics for thirty-eight years as of the 25th of last month, the day I thought I was going to be able to go home from this session. I have run in most of the elections that have come along since then and when I did not run in them myself I helped somebody else to do so. I have not missed any of them, and that means that there have only been three years since 1911 that I have not gone through an election campaign. Therefore I am not asking anybody to pass on information to me as to what happens in elections. I know pretty well what happens in elections. I also want to say that I have never once complained about how my constituency was drawn up, no matter who drew it up. I represented a seat in the Saskatchewan house for twenty-two and a half years or twenty-five sessions, and the only time my constituency was ever changed was during the period when the hon. member for Lake Centre was high in the councils of the Conservative party in the province of Saskatchewan.
Do you know what they did to me then? They took one of my best friends, who was

Somebody says that "crying" is the word. I might also say that we had -I was going to say "gerrymander" but I do not like that word; I do not even like "jimmymander"-a redistribution of seats in 1933 but it was not by the Liberals. I accept everything that the opposition has said to the effect that it would make no difference what party you had here or what government you had here they would do it just the same as this is being done. You know what happened after it was done by the Conservatives in 1933. We won almost as large a proportion of seats as we have now-almost as large a proportion of them; and the constituency which I represent now Mr. Motherwell represented. He won by a majority of 4,500- just a little less than I won it by the last time. After they had changed it and added on to it what they thought would give him some trouble he won the constituency. I have seen in the press recently a statement that is absolutely wrong, to the effect that they gerrymandered Mr. Motherwell out of this house. They did not do any such thing. Mr. Motherwell won the next election by 4,500. He was not gerrymandered out of anything, no matter what they tried to do.
We won most of the constituencies-16 out of 21 in Saskatchewan-on the Conservative redistribution. I am quite sure that if they were to make the redistribution now we would win more constituencies than we will after having made it ourselves-the reason being that you do not satisfy very many people when you are making a redistribution and those that you do satisfy never mention it any more. The only people who mention redistribution are those who do not like it, and they keep talking about it.
As far as I am concerned I would rather see the other fellows make the redistribution than make it ourselves; and for that reason this is the first time I ever made a speech in this house on redistribution. I would not be making one now if it were not for
TMr. Gardiner.]
the fact that so many misrepresentations have been made with regard to Saskatchewan.
I take the boundaries of the seat I run in as they are handed to me and I go out and try to win the votes of the people living in the constituency. I am not very much worried whether there are 50,000 or
30,000	or 40,000. I do not know which I prefer to have; but nevertheless I think when you are drafting constituencies of a province it ought to be done just as fairly as you can do it.
You know, I am going to say one thing which perhaps my friends think I should not say, but I am not so sure about that. I think it is reasonable to say it anyway. I have been in this house for seventeen years and there are two men I have marvelled at in that seventeen years. One of them was the last member for Haldimand and the other is the present member for Haldimand. I have said to people on this side of the house that there must be a lot of good people living in Haldimand because I do not know where you could get two better Grits, let alone two better Tories, than those men-as far as their relationships with the rest of us are concerned. Mr. Senn was the agricultural critic here for many years and he criticized our activities. Nevertheless, he was always fair and I found the same thing with regard to his successor. I regret, of course, that changes have taken place which make it necessary to have the representation of that area changed. I think everyone will agree that when you get down to a position where you have only half of the population you ought to have some change has got to be made.
The man who taught me to be a Liberal was the editor of the old paper up in Seaforth the Huron Expositor. His grandson is here a member. I used to read the old Huron Expositor as it was the only paper we could afford to have around on the farm. The editor was a good Grit and his editorials were all Liberal. I read them very carefully every week and they had an influence on me. I naturally regret that in this adjustment that is being made something has to be done with that constituency which some may not like. The two members in question made about as reasonable speeches in this discussion as we have heard in this house.
I want to say that after all I do not think we are going to do very much good to ourselves or to the country by getting up and shouting that all these things we have been doing ever since confederation have been wrong. I do not think they have been wrong. I think we are doing it just about as well as it can be done and I have sufficient

faith in the members of this house to think that none of them are ciphers. The suggestion was made that we have on committees men who are ciphers. But I do not think you can pick a cipher out of this house. There is no such thing here. We have members who can sit on committees and perform their duties in the manner in which members should and they take the responsibility for drafting constituencies in different provinces. Personally I think they have done as good a job as could have been done by a commission or any other kind of organization.

All we are saying is that this is a stupid method and that we should try another method.
If we take another method we are not taking a pig in a poke. I understand, and my information is, this has been used in England.
