I almost feel like starting it again, but I will not. I had just got to the point where I wanted to refer to statements made about this practice we are following and from here on I am going to try to be serious. I hope I will be allowed to be.
There are three or four comments which were made by the hon. member for Quebec South that I want to read. They are very brief, and as I read each of them I want hon. members of this committee to ask themselves whether or not what he says is correct. If what he says is correct then all I can say is that we should be ready to change this method. First of all I read his general comment from page 1808 of Hansard of 1939. He refers to what he calls:
. . . the procedure whereby every ten years or so this house is made the theatre of a somewhat unseemly, undignified and utterly confusing scramble for personal or political advantage.
Now, Mr. Chairman, either that is a clear description of what goes on, or it is not. I suggest that notwithstanding the disarming speech of the Minister of Agriculture that we listened to, there is, and is bound to be, a very considerable amount of truth in this remark made by the hon. member for Quebec South years ago. Later on he speaks about what he calls the law of the jungle, and he uses the phrase "might is right". I do not think anyone can doubt that even what I called the disarming speech of the Minister of Agriculture made perfectly clear that that is true; and therefore I ask, Mr. Chairman, whether it is reasonable, whether we as responsible people should be prepared to continue a method which is characterized in the way I have read, and I think fairly characterized.
We have been debating this now for three days. I do not know how much longer it is going to go on. I will not add much to it, but it will go on. As a matter of fact, when you come to think of it, Mr. Chairman, we are in a rather ridiculous position. There is no principle at all that we are following. I cannot find that there is any principle. The only principles that are mentioned have been ignored.
We had the old slogan of "representation by population" which is supposed to be the basis. We all recognize that there has to
[The Deputy Chairman.]
be some qualification of that, but how much qualification nobody knows. And so we get those fantastic results which have been pointed out. It is suggested there is give and take but as was pointed out here this morning, it is usually one side doing the giving and the other side doing the taking.
It occurred to me that it might be of interest to see whether any comment had been made in this country from which this gerrymander comes. I have here an article written by an American some years ago, and I want to quote from it very briefly because I think he describes very clearly what the effect of this is. His point is that it is really an evasion, a setting at naught of the democratic idea that representation should be by population.
That leads me to this point; it leads me to interject this. I hear people say that nobody in the country cares about this; nobody outside this house cares two straws about it.

The hon. member is covering quite a lot of territory when he says nobody said this. I am not suggesting he said it, but I have heard it said, and I have heard it said more than once; and my comment on it is that at the moment it may be true. There may not be very much interest in this throughout the country, but I believe that when people find out what has been happening there will be interest in the country. There will be great interest in Haldimand when they find out what has happened here, and I might mention other places, too. But I want to read now briefly from this statement which is found in the book entitled "American Political Science Review of 1918", which is a long time ago:
The gerrymander is an American name tor a political abuse, which, though by no means exclusively American, has been most widely practised and generally tolerated in this country. It is a device for the partial suppression of public opinion-
That I believe is worth thinking about; I believe it is true. I continue:
It is a device for the partial suppression of public opinion that simulates agreements with democratic institutions.
And further he says:
It is solely the accident of numerical superiority that determines which party is the offender and which the victim.
I think we can all say "amen" to that. I just wanted to raise these points. I imagine there will be more in this house who will agree with that than would like to say so. I can well imagine that some of those who have been occupied for some weeks in trying

to work things out might be among the first, if they felt free to do so, to say: Let us get some other plan.
As I said earlier, if we adopt the commission plan we are not taking something that is untried; we are taking something that has been tried elsewhere and is working, and I do not think any man in this house will say that he is satisfied with the present plan.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I should like at this time to congratulate those who sat on the redistribution committee for a job well done. As regards our two ridings in eastern Ontario, one of them, Glengarry, with a population of about 17,000 and Prescott, with a population edging 27,000, not much more could be done than to have a merger; and no happier marriage could have been thought of than to unite the two historic counties of Glengarry and Prescott.
As early as the year 1880, during the third parliament of confederation, the counties of Glengarry and Prescott were united through an act of parliament; and I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that the people I now have the honour to represent in this house welcome to their fold those of Glengarry, and I know that as much can be said for the population of the neighbouring riding now belonging to the new electoral district.
Two great nationalities have lived together in harmony since the beginning of our political history. Those of Scottish origin and people of French extraction 'have always lived happily together and have also, to use a French expression, "fait bon menage" with the Irish and English-speaking people.
The very word Glengarry calls up visions of chivalrous chieftains in waving tartans and plumed bonnets. It was after the suppression of the Jacobite rebellion of 1745 that the highlanders of old Glengarry in Scotland first emigrated to America settling, at the invitation of Sir William Johnson, in the Mohawk valley. It was a beautiful and fruitful land, but not for long did the highlanders give themselves to the quiet cultivation of their farms and orchards. The revolutionary storm was brewing when they arrived, and when it broke many of the Gaelic clansmen took up arms to strike for the king.
The war ended, and many of the highlanders settled in what are now the three counties of Glengarry, Stormont and Dundas. The government land agent allotted lands to them by letting them draw some numbered slips of paper shaken together in a hat. Amongst the newcomers were a number of highland gentlemen who had held commissions in the Royal Highland Emigrants and other regiments, and the half-pay received by these ex-officers was for some years the first
Redistribution
source of the very limited supply of cash which circulated in the settlements.
Sir John Johnson, who had lost an enormous amount of property, received some land in Glengarry. He built a mill at Williamstown, named after his father, and later presented to the people twelve acres for fair grounds which are still in use under the name of the Glengarry agricultural grounds.
In the first parliament of Upper Canada, two Macdonell brothers sat for Glengarry and one of them was elected Speaker. The famous Glengarry Regiment of Light Infantry which so distinguished itself through the war of 1812 was raised chiefly through the exertions of the two other men of that name; and a Macdonell shared the fate and the glory of Brock in the battle of Queenston Heights. Yet another Macdonell, a priest, Alexander, came from Inverness in 1786 with almost his whole parish of about 500 souls, to found in the new Glengarry St. Raphael's, the pioneer parish of his communion in Upper Canada. Here he built the first Roman Catholic church known as the blue chapel upon the site of which another priest of the same name, who became the first Roman Catholic bishop in Upper Canada, erected a large and handsome church.
Later, when war with the United States was threatening, the future bishop, actuated by patriotic motives, was more active in rousing and recruiting the Glengarries. But by no means were his energies devoted to military affairs. As a missionary the sphere of his labours extended over a great part of Upper Canada. For instance, immediately after his arrival in this country he made it his business to obtain legal patents for the lands held by the highlanders. The "man from Glengarry" had the reputation of being strong and forceful and it is said that the history of the county is a proud record of most valuable services rendered to the county in early times when the men of that county made its name famous in war and peace.
Prescott county, set apart in 1798 and named after the governor of Canada who succeeded Lord Dorchester, has special links with the French regime. There is a tradition that the rude little fort at the foot of the Long Sault rapids on the Ottawa, where Dollard des Ormeaux, with his sixteen heroic Frenchmen, made his stand against the Iroquois, was at Greece's Point in Hawkes-bury township.
The township of Longueuil represents one of the very few grants made during the French regime, on the feudal system, within the limits of what is now Ontario. On a map of 1828 it was marked as the seigniory of

Redistribution
Pointe a l'Orignal. It was owned by descendants of Charles Le Moyne, elder brother of the famous d'Iberville, but in 1796 was sold to an American named Treadwell who opened it to emigrants.
Both United Empire Loyalists and Americans who sympathized with the other side in the struggle with Britain were numerous among the Prescott pioneers. Settlers of French origin cultivated the low-lying lands and also helped to build up the county. During the war of 1812, at which period the county was grouped with its southern neighbour Glengarry for parliamentary representation, Prescott men of both races fought for England.
In 1805 a mill was erected in Hawkesbury which was bought three years afterward by three brothers named Hamilton. One has since become a senator and another was in succession bishop of Niagara and of Ottawa.
The parish of Hawkesbury originally included the whole of Prescott county, but in 1869 the two parishes of Vankleek Hill and Plantagenet were set off from it. L'Orignal, the French word for moose, is still the county seat. Formerly most of its inhabitants were English but the great majority are now French. It is an historic little village, on the shore of the Ottawa river. At first the court sat in a schoolhouse, and a private house, generally the sheriff's, was used for a jail.
To have been a member of the first Canadian parliament and represented the riding of Prescott in the Commons under the premierships of Sir John A. Macdonald, 1867-1873, and Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, 1873-1878, was the distinction of Mr. Albert Hagar. When the first session of the new federal parliament opened on November 8, 1867, Mr. Hagar was 40 years of age. He was also in the Commons chamber on the tragically memorable night of April 6, 1868, when Hon. Thomas D'Arcy McGee, famous Irish orator, writer, patriot and statesman, made his last speech a few hours before he fell victim to an assassin's bullet. It was a dramatic incident in the history of the nascent Canadian nation that Mr. Hagar vividly recalled on occasion when in a reminiscent mood.
Mr. Hagar and Sir Mackenzie Bowell, who was Canada's sixth premier and held that office from 1894 to 1896, were roommates. No railways linked Ottawa and Montreal by direct route in those far-away pioneer days, and the first member for Prescott used to make the forty-mile trip from his home in Plantagenet to the capital to attend to his sessional duties by sleigh in winter and by
[Mr. Bruneau.l
boat in summer. This trip he would undertake weekly during the session, no matter how severe the weather.
The constituency of Glengarry-Prescott will now constitute a wedge in the whole eastern tip of Ontario bordering the province of Quebec between the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa rivers. This fraternity of people of different denomination and racial origin will, I am sure, as it has in the past, have its bearing on the development of our great country, and will leave its imprint on our national history.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is appropriate that on this Dominion day we should be debating the subject of redistribution in the various provinces of Canada. For a while we heard a discussion respecting Ontario. Then we shifted to the west, where we dealt in some detail with the problem in Saskatchewan. From the hon. member who has just taken his seat we heard a most interesting discussion of the historical background of two of the older constituencies in Ontario.
Then in the course of the debate this afternoon we heard the most optimistic survey I have heard for some time as to the possibilities of the Conservative party in Saskatchewan. I only hope the Minister of Agriculture is as sound in his diagnosis of the position of that party in Saskatchewan as I think he was unsound in his diagnosis of the lines that should be drawn in that province.
For a short time I should like to discuss the situation as it affects one of the most easterly provinces of Canada, the province of Nova Scotia. I do this because some reference has been made to that province and to one or more constituencies during the debate which has progressed during the last two days.
It is a matter of record, to be found by looking at the bill, that the representation of this province is to be reduced at this time. It will be recalled that at one time the province of Nova Scotia had 21 members in this House of Commons, and we are now to lose one of our present members. It is true that we are losing one which we gained, but we will be back to 12 members despite the fact that the census indicates an increase in population of some 64,000 to 66,000. In other words our population has increased more than the quotient which is necessary for the election of a member. However, because of the increase in other parts of Canada it is found necessary to reduce the representation of this province by one member.

I agree with what the Minister of Agriculture said this morning about hon. members welcoming and supporting the formula which prevented a marked reduction in the representation of certain provinces. We supported that; we believed it was necessary and right. But we rather wish that some formula could have been devised which would have prevented the representation of this province, which has suffered such a marked reduction through the years, being still further reduced at this time. This is not because of any decrease in population; it is despite the fact that there has been a substantial increase in the population of the province.
Having made those general remarks, I should like to look for a moment at the redistribution of seats within the province. There are bound to be anomalies in such a distribution. For instance, there is Cape Breton island with a large industrial city, having a population of over 80,000. Then there are rural seats with populations substantially less. I do not think any consideration was given nor should it have been given to a redistribution in that particular area. It is separate and apart from the rest of the province. It has a huge industrial area; and although the populations of other ridings are not in proportion, there are areas there which make redistribution difficult.
Then coming to the mainland we find a tremendous increase in the population of Halifax with no change being made in that riding. This is one of the two dual ridings in Canada. When one realizes the disparity between the populations of these different ridings he can appreciate the argument-in fact it was more than an argument, it was more or less a prophecy that was made by one hon. gentleman-that this is probably the last redistribution we will have by the House of Commons, that within the next decade steps will have been taken to provide the method which has been suggested during this debate and thereby overcome the anomalies which undoubtedly exist.
Let me deal briefly for a moment with ridings apart from those I have mentioned. According to the last census report supplied by the department the smallest riding in the province, the one which I shall deal with first, has a population of 26,212, indicating an increase of only 210 in population during the last decade. The second riding has a population of 26,936 with an increase of 1,700 during the last decade. The largest rural riding in the province, Annapolis-Kings, has a population of 54,930, with an
Redistribution
increase of over 8,300 during the last decade. The riding of Annapolis-Kings showed the largest increase of any riding with the exception of the city and county of Halifax. It is one of the two rural ridings in the province which is above the quotient of 54,000 which is needed. That was the situation that existed when the committee came to consider what action should be taken.
A committee was set up which considered these various factors. It was faced with the fact that one seat had to be removed from the province. It was decided that the riding which should be dropped was the second smallest in the province, the one with a population of 26,936. That riding was done away with at the committee meeting. After considering all the factors involved in the situation the committee decided that the constituency of Annapolis-Kings should remain as is and that the population of this riding which was being removed-

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: On a question of privilege, I was chairman of the subcommittee of that province and no such agreement was entered into.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I knew this question of privilege would be raised; I knew there would be an abuse of the question of privilege to which you, Mr. Chairman, objected a little while ago and to which your predecessor had earlier objected. If the hon. gentleman wishes to make a speech in connection with it, it is his privilege to do so. I am giving my word as a member of this house that the definite decision was arrived at in that committee that the constituency of Annapolis-Kings should be left alone. That is supported by other members of the committee who were with me, not only Conservative members but others as well.
Be that as it may, as I said weeks went by and finally the report was shown to me. I then found that the municipality of Digby had been added to Annapolis-Kings. So we arrived at this situation. The smallest constituency in the province, Antigonish-Guys-borough, with 26,212 remains unchanged, yet 11,508 of population is added to the largest rural constituency in the province, giving it a population of 66,500 odd.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: That is a shame.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I am not questioning that; I simply want to bring out these facts because we are discussing the manner in which redistribution has been carried on. The suggestion has been made that some other system would work more effectively, and I suggest that these facts corroborate that suggestion. The largest constituency receives this addition while the smallest constituency remains as is.

Redistribution
It may be said that there were political difficulties in removing the small constituency. I am quite prepared to admit that there were difficulties, but I do suggest that it is a rather anomalous situation when you find this disparity. It rather bears out the statement found in the new testament where the Saviour said, "To him that hath shall be given." Certainly that was the case here, because one of the largest constituencies had more given to it.
It is true that yesterday the minister, in replying to a statement made by the hon. member for Kamloops, said the constituency of Lunenburg had received a greater addition than any other constituency in the province. It is true that the constituency of Lunenburg received 12,544 additional votes and that the constituency of Annapolis-Kings received 11,580. In other words, the constituency of Lunenburg got 964 more people than the constituency of Annapolis-Kings. But you start off with the constituency of Lunenburg with a population of 33,256, and you start off with the constituency of Annapolis-Kings with a population of 54,930. Therefore the argument about having received such an increase is not quite so effective as one might think.
Alternative suggestions were made. I am not going to labour the matter at this time. The net result of redistribution in so far as these three constituencies in the southwestern part of the province are concerned is as follows. The new constituency of Queens-Lunenburg will have a population of 45,800; the constituency of Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare will have a population of 45,595, and the constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings will have a population of 66,510. In other words, after redistribution there is a disparity of over 21,000 between the constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings and the other two constituencies to which I have referred.
I am suggesting that is not redistribution as it should be. Some system could have been worked out. We have finally decided to divide counties on the basis of municipalities, and if that suggestion had been adopted the constituency of Annapolis-Kings would still have been larger than either of the other two but the disparity would have been a matter of 4,000 or 5,000 instead of over 21,000.
We have heard discussions today about urban ridings in Saskatchewan with a population of 45,000 or 50,000, and we have heard discussions about rural ridings in Ontario with populations of 50,000 and much less. If you describe a rural constituency as one containing no cities within its boundaries, then
[Mr. Nowlan.l
I say the net result of this redistribution in Nova Scotia is that in Digby-Annapolis-Kings you have the largest rural constituency in Canada with a population of 66,500.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: That is not so.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
The hon. gentlemen say it is not so. They can produce their figures. I have checked the records and I believe that to be a true statement. I could have made a mistake in checking the records. I was certain of what happened in the committee, but I am prepared to be corrected with respect to the report of the census commission, though I went through it and could not find any other riding in Canada not containing a city which had a population as large as that. However, if there is one, well and good. It will certainly be an exception. I know that if the committee report that was first brought in had been adopted this situation would not have prevailed, and one would not have to talk about it now. I should like to know why the decision made by the committee was not acted upon and why for some reason there were no subsequent meetings of the committee whatsoever until objection was taken.
In saying what I have said, may I say that I have heard some members discussing the situation in the constituency of Annapolis-Kings. I presume there are slips of the tongue but some almost seemed to speak in such a way as to assume that one has a vested right in a constituency. I want to make it abundantly plain that I am not seeking to create any such impression in so far as the constituency of which I am the member at the present time is concerned. No candidates have been nominated by any party. I do not know when they will be nominated, nor do I know who will be nominated, and certainly I would be the last to suggest who might be elected because that is the prerogative of the people of the constituency and certainly not one which anyone can assume.
In speaking as I have this afternoon I want to explain that I am not speaking at all because of any personal implications whatsoever. I am speaking on behalf of the people of that constituency who I think are going to be placed in a most invidious position in the future in so far as representation is concerned, no matter what member of what party may represent it. If I were a candidate again and it were my good fortune to be elected I would be very happy to represent as well as I could the people of this whole constituency, both Annapolis-Kings and the Digby addition. It is an honour to anyone to represent a constituency in which he has

lived and which he has adopted as is the case so far as I am concerned with respect to Annapolis-Kings.
In so far as Digby is concerned, if I should be elected to represent it I would be elected by the county in which I was born, because Digby county is the place of my birth. It is true that it is just outside of the municipality which has been added to the constituency, but it is so near the boundary that one can almost throw a stone across it, and the school I attended as a very small boy is the school that is established within this municipality. I well remember as a very young boy going to Weymouth, which is in the constituency, and being amazed and enthralled at the signs of industrial activity I saw there. There were a few sawmills and some schooners lying at the wharf. In those days Digby of course was an industrial centre which was almost as remote and certainly more important than Boston, which was the centre of the maritime provinces as far as we were concerned at that time.
As I have said, one could welcome from every standpoint of tradition and sentiment the representation of that constituency. My forefathers established their homes there. Their names have been associated for generations with the development of the county as stipendiary magistrates and municipal councillors. Therefore I say that from the standpoint of tradition and sentiment I welcome the opportunity to represent a constituency which now includes the municipality of the county of my birth as well as that part of the constituency which was mine by adoption.
But, sir, how can it be done adequately when the population is so large? Some talk was heard in the committee about the fact that there were many long miles of coast line which it was very difficult to represent in the House of Commons. I quite admit there are difficulties in representing fishing communities. We all know that. I have them in my own constituency as it exists today, and although there may not be the deep indentations along the coast line of Annapolis-Kings that there are in the Yarmouth or Shelburne districts, my impression would be that there are just as many fishing communities along these smaller indentations in the coast line as there are along the much deeper ones in the other counties.
After all, one is not elected to this house to represent scenery or miles of beautiful highways. It is a question of representing the people who live along those highways. It is a matter of representing the population, whether along the seacoast or in the interior. Take the constituency of
Redistribution
Annapolis-Kings. It is approximately 112 miles from Hantsport to Weymouth along the highway. In addition there are five parallel systems of highways running east and west down through Kings county including the trunk highway and over to the bay shore. It is true that when you get down into Annapolis county you only have two, but in addition you have all the crossroads running back and forth. All the fishing communities, the apple growers and dairy farmers, and now the lumbermen and other fishermen of Digby county, have to be represented. No matter how efficient a member may be, whoever may be elected, no matter how conscientious he may be, it is going to be most difficult for him to give to the people of that constituency the representation which they deserve and which they need. I do suggest that a system of redistribution could have been followed, sir, which would have given more equality of representation and which would have been fairer to the people involved than the one which has been adopted and carried out.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was not a member of the committee, and I thought perhaps somebody might ask me why I am speaking on this occasion. I expected the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings would make the remarks he has made. I was led to that expectation by reports from the members of the committee as well as by reports in the press.
I am satisfied, Mr. Chairman, that what was done by the committee was done in the best interests of Nova Scotia. Perhaps it might be well in the few minutes remaining before four o'clock to give a brief review.
In the 1947 redistribution on the basis of 1941 figures, the Nova Scotia population was 577,962. The 1951 census showed us to have a population of 642,548, an increase of 64,622 or 11-2 per cent. The corresponding increase for Canada for the same period is 17-5 per cent, which means that although Nova Scotia gained 64,622 in population we lose one seat.
As the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings has said, our representation in this house has varied, quite widely since confederation. At the date of confederation, 1867, we had 19 members; that rose to 21 members in 1872; it remained at 21 members in 1882. Then we started to decline. In 1889 we had 20; in 1903, 18; 1914, 16; 1925, 14; 1933, 12; and in 1947 we went up to 13 members. In this redistribution we go back to 12 members.
It is interesting to note here that the committee has recommended a return to the precise constituency boundary arrangement that prevailed after the redistribution of 1933 which of course, as hon. members will recall,

Redistribution
was done under a Conservative government. In Nova Scotia at the present time we have 12 constituencies with 13 members, Halifax being a dual constituency. Following this redistribution we will have 11 constituencies with 12 members. At the present time representation of the constituencies is: eight constituencies represented by nine Liberals; three constituencies represented by three Progressive Conservatives; and one constituency represented by a C.C.F. member.
It has been said that in every redistribution somebody is bound to be hurt. Well, Mr. Chairman, the only people who are going to be injured in this redistribution are the people of Queens-Shelburne, who will sacrifice the services of one of the finest members that has ever represented them in the House of Commons.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: It has been the practice of opposition members in this debate to refer to their members, perhaps with reason, as being without exception distinguished members.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Outstanding.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Quite outstanding. I wish to say here that when we are talking about distinguished members in the House of Commons the present member for Queens-Shelburne is the peer of anybody. On that basis I say the only people in Nova Scotia who stand to be hurt are the people of Queens-Shelburne who will be deprived of the privilege of being represented by that distinguished member.
A look at the map of Nova Scotia by anyone who is observant will show that the three constituencies represented by Progressive Conservatives in one way or another adjoin each other. There were possible ways of redistributing Nova Scotia so that these three seats would become two seats. It was felt by members of the committee, and I concurred of course, that the arrangement that would cause the least disturbance to voters in Nova Scotia generally would be a reversion to what took place in 1933 under the Progressive Conservative government.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Just Conservative then.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Just as a matter of interest I read some of the debates on that occasion. The chairman of the committee was Mr. R. K. Smith, who represented Cumberland. He was justifying the constituency set-up at that time, the same one we are proposing now, and he said:
In effect, all that has happened to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis is this. He has had a small portion cut off the western end of his constituency namely, Clare, and he has had a larger portion
(Mr. Winters.]
added to the eastern end, namely, Kings. It is unfortunate, I admit, that this constituency is larger than desirable in population and area, and no one regrets it more than I do, but we had to come to that conclusion under the circumstances. Somebody in the province of Nova Scotia had to get hurt in this redistribution: some one had to make a sacrifice, and in the layout and recasting that presented itself to me I felt that the sacrifice would have to be made where recommended.
Exactly the same conditions prevail here, and another sacrifice had to be made. It seemed to be the fair thing. And I must say in all honesty and sincerity that I was never more surprised than at the objection coming from the member for Annapolis-Kings, when it was decided that a seat would have to be dropped and when the committee recommended, I think with justification, that it should be a Liberal seat that should be dropped. Despite the distinguished representation here in the house, there was a population of 26,936 that had to be absorbed.
I should say here that the new constituency of Queens-Lunenburg will reflect a greater increase in both population and area than any other constituency in Nova Scotia.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have heard from several quarters that the pressing of this bill is impeding the progress of the business of the house which all hon. members want to complete. I feel that the bill has had ample discussion. I do not think anything can be clarified more than it has been clarified. I submit that we should go ahead and pass this bill. We could do it in ten minutes, and the business of the house would be completed that much more quickly.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: Right or wrong, pass it! That is not good business.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
I was discussing this bill at nine o'clock on June 24. It is really so long ago that I have almost forgotten. Before I continue with my remarks may I say that I have been asked by the hon. member for Lambton West to make for him a correction in his remarks here some time ago when he was discussing the Boundary Pipeline Corporation bill. At that time he said that about 2J billion cubic feet a year were coming back into Canada from the United States, and that was coming in through the province of Ontario. This was a mistake as far as the number of cubic feet were concerned. During the calendar year 1950 3 billion cubic feet came into the province of Ontario. In the calendar year 1951 3-3 billion cubic feet were received. At the present time the Union Gas Company are receiving at a daily rate which will ensure receipt of the 5J billion cubic feet this calendar year which is covered by their contract and the export permit granted by the federal power commission in the United States. The hon. member for Lamb-ton West wished me to make that correction for him.
When I was discussing this matter the other evening I stated what I thought was in the interests of the people in my part of the dominion. While we do not expect to obtain any great benefit from this great natural resource in the province of Alberta, we are nevertheless concerned that it be preserved for the people of Canada. That is the chief reason I am speaking tonight. Also at this time I should like to commend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra for the great interest he has taken in this matter. I know that the only interest the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has in trying to protect this great natural resource for the people of Canada is the interest he has in the future of this country.
At 9 o'clock last Tuesday night I was discussing the policy of the United States. At that time I was comparing the policy there with what I thought should be the policy here in Canada. In the United States the government protects its people in the exportation of gas; that is, if they consider there is not sufficient gas for exportation and for the use of their own people in the United States, then they prohibit the export of gas to Canada. In that connection I had read a paragraph from the decision in the Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line Company case re the application of the Union Gas Company of the city of Toronto. If further evidence is necessary-and I think perhaps it would do no harm to produce further evidence-
Boundary Pipeline Corporation I should like to read section 3 of the Natural Gas Act of the United States:
After six months from June 21, 1938, no person shall export any natural gas from the United States to a foreign country or import any natural gas from a foreign country without first having secured an order of the commission authorizing it to do so. The commission shall issue such order upon application, unless, after opportunity for hearing, it finds that the proposed exportation or importation will not be consistent with the public interest.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that the first consideration of the government of the United States is their own public interest. To continue:
The commission may by its order grant such application, in whole or in part, with such modification and upon such terms and conditions as the commission may find necessary or appropriate, and may from time to time, after opportunity for hearing, and for good cause shown, make such supplemental order in the premises as it may find necessary or appropriate.
This act was passed on June 21, 1938. As I stated before, that is the practice in the United States with regard to the exportation of gas. There must be an order from the federal power commission. This order is subject to cancellation upon proof of an unsatisfied need for gas in territories adjacent to the pipe line in the United States. As far as we are concerned, Mr. Chairman, I think that is sufficient evidence that the United States does not intend to export this great natural resource to Canada. Naturally they could not export it to any other country, unless it would be Mexico or South America because, as we know, the only way in which gas can be exported is by pipe line. It is not like gasoline, as one of the hon. members here mentioned the other night. Gasoline or oil can be exported by boats, by tank cars and in many different ways. And besides protecting their own interests as far as their export of gas is concerned, the large gas pipe line companies in the United States also wish to protect their own market against imported gas from other countries. We might almost say that they want it both ways.
The Pacific Northwest Pipe Line Company, which is controlled by the Fish Engineering Corporation in the United States, as is the Boundary Pipeline company, is opposing the export of gas from Canada through the province of British Columbia. The other evening the hon. member for Kindersley mentioned the fact that we are already exporting gas. Well, it is a fact that we have already arranged to export and hope to arrange for the further export of gas to Seattle and Portland, but this large United States company is trying to prevent the export of Canadian gas to the United States at the present

Boundary Pipeline Corporation time because, as I say, they want to reserve that splendid market for themselves.
It is well known that we export gas at the present time, some 10 billion cubic feet a year, to Montana to be used by the Anaconda Company there.
I should like to read a quotation from the Sunday Sun of Vancouver, dated June 14, which says:
Gas reserves key to pipe-line permit
This article mentions the fact that it is hoped gas will be exported from the Peace river area through British Columbia and into the western United States. It is practically the only market we would have for the gas from the Peace river area, besides serving local needs.
The article goes on:
Big rival of Westcoast in securing the necessary United States Pacific northwest markets is Pacific Northwest Pipelines Incorporated, a company affiliated with the Fish Engineering Corporation, Houston, Texas, well known in the gas transmission industry. It wants to pipe Texas gas to Portland and Seattle.
Pacific Northwest Pipelines have secured the allegiance of Henry Gellert, president of the Seattle Gas Company, who has declined to give Westcoast even a letter of intent to purchase Canadian gas.
These forces will oppose Westcoast before the FPC.
At the board hearings in the past three days they were represented by S. Bruce Smith, Q.C. of Edmonton, who battled long and hard with cross examinations to prove that Peace river gas reserves are not sufficient, that Westcoast is not financially sound in its backing, that it should have firm commitments from gas suppliers and distributors before any permit is granted by the board.
The board was satisfied in all requirements excepting that of the problem of gas reserves.
I quote that to show to what ends the gas companies in the United States will go to try to retain their own markets. I quoted the former references to show just how difficult it is for us to obtain gas from the United States, if they consider their own people are not being fully served.
I do not wish to repeat what I said on a former occasion, but it has been shown to this committee that both Ontario and Quebec are well acquainted with the fact that it is very difficult indeed to secure gas from the United States. They realize that the government of the United States is averse to shipping gas into Canada unless, as I said a moment ago, all their people are served along the different pipe lines that have already been constructed. Evidence was adduced in this committee to show that along most of the pipe lines from Texas to the Canadian border there is still a great demand in the United States for gas. The gas companies of Ontario realize this, and they also realize that if they are to have in the


future a permanent supply of gas they cannot depend on the United States for it. They must depend on the gas which comes from the province of Alberta. This has been stated definitely by the officials in the government of the province of Ontario and very emphatically by the premier of Quebec, who said that if his province is to obtain gas anywhere he is determined that it shall be from an Alberta source, because he believes it is the only sure source from which a guaranteed supply for the future can be drawn.
I want to commend also the Alberta resources board. I believe they are anxious to supply the Canadian market. They are anxious to supply the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, but before doing so they are investigating the supply of natural gas in their own province. That is a very wise decision. The Trans-Canada company already has a charter to build a pipe line across Canada which would supply both Ontario and Quebec. In connection with the Trans-Canada pipe line I should like to read a quotation from the Globe and Mail of January 22, 1952, which gives the attitude of Mr. Gem-mell, who is the minister of mines of the province of Ontario. This article has been quoted before in this house. After mentioning why they wish Alberta gas the article goes on:
For these reasons, the Alberta petroleum resources board is giving long consideration to the Delhi application for permission to pipe gas to Ontario and Quebec. Some experts say Alberta has plenty of gas and to spare but the board is investigating. And when and if the Alberta board gives the pipe line the nod, its promoters must next get permission from the board of transport commissioners here to build the line. It is thought, however, that if the Alberta board agrees, the transport commissioners will not make any difficulties.
An alternative suggestion, Mr. Gemmell said, is that if Alberta would allow gas to be piped into the western United States, Ontario might draw an equal volume from the Texas wells. Gas is now being piped north from Texas to Detroit and thence into Windsor and western Ontario.
Mr. Gemmell declared the provincial government was wholly opposed to any deal of this kind. In the first place, he said, it was very doubtful that the United States authorities would agree to supply Ontario with a firm uninterrupted volume of gas.
That is the situation as far as these great provinces of Ontario and Quebec are concerned. It is not necessary for me to point out the great need of this natural resource in the large provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
Those who are in favour of this Boundary Pipeline bill state that they are to supply gas to Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Evidence and arguments have been produced to show that this line would not be feasible. The chief argument against it is its size. It would be only a 16-inch pipe line whereas Trans-Canada pipe line would be 30 inches. The

difference in capacity between a 16-inch pipe line and a 30-inch line is in the ratio of one to three and a half. It would be impossible for Boundary Pipeline to supply Ontario and Quebec, as well as Manitoba and other places, even if it were not the intention of the company- and we submit it is the intention- to pipe this gas into the United States. As I say, even if that were not the intention of the company, we contend that a line of this size would not supply Ontario and Quebec. Another line would have to be built, thus greatly increasing the cost of gas not only to the people this line proposes to supply but to the people purchasing gas in Ontario and Quebec.
As far as I am concerned, personally I hold no brief for any company; but I do believe that Trans-Canada has the right idea in that already they have provided themselves with large areas in Alberta capable of producing gas. Boundary Pipeline has no gas areas of its own. Trans-Canada has undertaken to build a pipe line in this country at a cost of about $350 million, and this would give a tremendous amount of work to the people of this country. It would also mean that in those great areas at the head of the lakes the pulp companies would have the opportunity to use this natural gas.
I was deeply impressed by the speech of the hon. member for Calgary West on May 2 of this year. I do not suppose there is anyone in the house who knows more than he does about this situation. He has made a thorough study of the production of gas in his own province, so when he speaks he speaks with authority. I am not going to read what he said, but hon. members will see that at page 1836 of Hansard he pointed out that Boundary Pipeline is condemned first of all on account of its limited size, to which I have already made reference.
He pointed out further that it opened up only a limited market. If there are the great quantities of gas in Alberta which we think there are, then it is not a limited market we want. We want opened up the great markets of Ontario and Quebec, and other parts of Canada. He also pointed out it would cost the consumers in Saskatchewan and Manitoba more because of the small size of the pipe. He added the irrefutable argument that the building of this small pipe line might delay for years the building of a larger one capable of serving Ontario and Quebec.
I have said that, as opposed to the Boundary pipe line, there is the Trans-Canada with three and a half times the capacity. Trans-Canada is a company which to a great extent has already made provision for
Boundary Pipeline Corporation the transportation of the gas, and has the financial backing to carry it through.
Another phase brought very much to the fore by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra not only in the consideration of this pipe line but also in that of others, is our Canada first policy. I can see nothing wrong with a Canada first policy. We in Canada have great natural resources. I do not suppose there is any country in the world with resources to equal ours, and there seems to be no reason why we should not try to conserve those resources for our own people. In the early days when Canada was a new country we did not have the financial institutions we have today. There was not available the great financial backing we now find in this country. At that time we did allow our natural resources to be exported to a much greater extent than they should have been. I believe that today there should be more manufacturing in this country of our own raw materials. If we conserve our resources and manufacture our raw materials we will build up our own industry and, better than that, we will build up our country.

The thirties have nothing to do with it. When we talk about our natural resources we must go back to the time the country was settled. It is our duty as Canadian citizens to conserve those resources not only for ourselves but for future generations. Unless we do so we can never be the great country we were intended to be.
In the early days of the United States when they did not have the financial backing to build their own industry, the New England colonies and other states shipped their natural resources to England. The United States did not become a great country until she began to manufacture. The same is true of the southern United States. We have heard how in days gone by they exported their cotton to other parts of the world so that the southern United States remained the poor section of that country. But that condition did not continue when they began manufacturing their cotton.
In common with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, I do not think any apology should be made in the house or anywhere else in Canada for advocating a Canada first policy so far as our natural resources are concerned.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
How would the hon. member relate the theory he is now expounding to the

Boundary Pipeline Corporation importation of bauxite, upon which our aluminum industry is one hundred per cent dependent?

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
I am not saying Canada should not import bauxite or any other raw material from any other country. If another country wishes to export its raw material to Canada, that is perfectly all right so far as I am concerned. But the fact that some other country wishes to export its raw material is no logical reason for stating that we should do the same. I know the hon. member comes from British Columbia, and that out there they are developing a great aluminum industry. I congratulate the hon. member and his province upon having that great industry there. But, so far as I can see, that is no reason why we should export all our raw materials such as pulpwood, iron ore and other products out of this country in order that some other country might become prosperous.
I see that my time is practically up but, as I said a moment ago, I do not believe it is in the best interests of this country that this bill should pass and a franchise be granted to the Boundary Pipeline Corporation to build a pipe line from the Alberta oil fields to the province of Manitoba.

Mr. Chairman, it is with pleasure that the province of Quebec, which is at present experiencing the most phenomenal industrial development in her history, if not in the whole history of Canada, finds that a sister province, the province of Alberta, is also going through a period of prosperity and progress.
In Alberta, oil and gas may be considered as the two main factors of this new and truly prodigious era. In the province of Quebec, the causes appear to be more diversified and more numerous. There is obviously the Ungava iron ore, but one must not forget our copper, zinc and lead mines, our gold, titanium and asbestos mines, our pulp and paper production, our almost inexhaustible hydroelectric resources. One must not forget either another very important factor, namely, a very active, progressive, judicious and far-sighted provincial administration.

There is a time for everything. It is commonly known that we, from the province of Quebec, jealously defend our province's rights and intend to protect and keep them at any cost. However, this does not prevent us from understanding the economic interdependence of the various provinces, or from surmising that in ensuring a better future to the province of Quebec, we also ensure a brighter future not only to our immediate neighbours but to all those who belong to the Canadian confederation.
Besides, the whole of the Canadian press has shown some interest in the new Quebec developments. The newspapers have dispatched observers to Ungava, Gaspe, the Chibougamau area, Sept lies, Havre St. Pierre and other places. Why have they done it? Because people are ready to admit that what benefits Quebec will benefit, directly or indirectly, the rest of the country.
I trust that the citizens of Alberta, like those of the province of Quebec, wish to contribute not only to the prosperity of their own province but to the welfare of Canada as a whole.
Now I believe that in granting the request contained in Bill No. 62 to incorporate the Boundary Pipeline Corporation, we would serve the interests of others before the interests of Canada. Why? Because the new company plans on laying a pipe line which would run from Alberta across Saskatchewan and Manitoba and then, instead of con-

tinuing eastward toward Ontario and Quebec, would go south into the United States.
Now, why would we supply American cities and states with natural gas before supplying our own cities and provinces? Is it not true that charity begins at home? Would it not be more logical for Alberta to sell her products in Canada first? Especially when many parts of the country are in need of natural gas!
Business is business, of course. However, if I can be successful and at the same time help my brothers why should I give preference to foreigners? A matter of patriotism and national unity is involved in this bill. National unity calls for mutual assistance, co-operation between the provinces whilst patriotism requires each one of us to favour first of all our fellow countrymen, our fellow citizens.
There are some people, businessmen, industrial leaders, who, as soon as they walk into their office, cast aside all concern for the welfare of the nation. They claim to be good Canadians and even, sometimes, great Canadians. But as soon as money enters into the picture they forget those high principles they so loudly proclaim at every opportunity.
I do not claim that the promoters of this company are that kind of Canadians. I consider, however, that they are making a mistake and the legislator is duty bound, under the circumstances, to call them to order and to prevent them from doing what would be detrimental to the public interest.
Would it mean that, by adopting such an attitude, we want to express a certain measure of animosity against the United States? Certainly not, and it would be ridiculous to think so. The good neighbour policy between Canada and the United States is something wonderful, something unique in this world, I would say. It should and will be preserved for all sorts of excellent reasons.
The Canadian humourist, Stephen Leacock, pointed out one day that we were wasting so much time explaining to the English that we were not Americans and to the Americans that we were not English, that there remained scarcely any time for us to be real Canadians.
I am convinced that now the Americans know and understand us much better, particularly since the last few years. If Mr. Leacock were still living, he would doubtlessly hasten to correct his assertion, which somehow has become less true now. Today the Americans and the British are informed
Boundary Pipeline Corporation about us and we have much more time to behave as true Canadians. And that is what the members of this house who have objected to Bill 62 have done.
Will the Americans resent it? Will they show any spite? Not at all. And everyone knows quite well they would be the first to do the same. We want to co-operate with them and no doubt they wish to offer us their fullest co-operation. Nevertheless, both sides, of course, will look first of all after their own interests. It is normal, it is fair, it is sensible.
Providence has been kind to us in allowing us to live in Canada, where the soil and underground are probably the richest in the world. It is true that at one time there were some who would not believe in the great resources of Canada.
Voltaire, as you well know, had no admiration for Canada and this is what he wrote in chapter twenty-three of his book Candide, published nearly two centuries ago:
"Who are all these people?"

speechtext: Is Voltaire not on the Index?

Perhaps, but the paragraph I will quote certainly is not. The hon. member will understand it perfectly.
. . . said Candide on the Dutch vessel. "Something quite silly and quite abominable," replied Martin. "You know England; are people there as silly as in France?" "It is another kind of folly," said Martin. "As you know, those two countries are at war over a few acres of snow in the direction of Canada and they are spending for this fine war much more than Canada is worth."
So it was England who inherited these few acres of snow. Nevertheless, in 1816, a large number of Britishers were quite ready to believe that Canada was a very poor conquest.
Was it not Mr. Alex Baring, later Lord Ashburton, who, in that year, wrote Mr. John Q. Adams, then American ambassador to London, the following words:
"I wish the British government would give you Canada at once. It is fit for nothing but to breed quarrels."
Fortunately, Baring's advice was not followed and Canada did not fall into American hands.
Indeed, little by little, it was realized that this country had tremendous possibilities. Even in 1842, Charles Dickens wrote the following in his "American Notes":
"It is full of hope and promise."
And the first years of the twentieth century, which, according to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was to be Canada's century brought an era

Boundary Pipeline Corporation of progress and change. For instance, it was in 1903, while the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway was being built, that silver ore was discovered in the Cobalt district. The development of our mines was then to be ceaselessly carried out all through Canada, in the east, west, north and1 south.
That is how natural gas was discovered in Alberta. According to statistics for the year 1949, according to the Canada Year Book, 1951, page 520 of the English edition, Alberta produced approximately 85 per cent of Canada's natural gas. In 1949, total production in all provinces amounted to 60 billion cubic feet, of which 51 billion cubic feet were produced in Alberta. Ontario's production in 1949 was but 8 billion cubic feet.
It can therefore be said that Alberta is truly the producer of natural gas. It is undoubtedly a great honour, but an honour that entails heavy responsibilities. Needless to say, Alberta cannot use all that gas and must export some. I do not object to her exporting it first to the neighbouring provinces. But we believe that she should then think of the other provinces-although they may be a little farther-that could benefit from Alberta's natural gas transported by way of a pipe line.
People in the other provinces, and more particularly in Ontario and Quebec, cannot understand why it has been decided to build a pipe line which, instead of serving them, would branch off towards the United States. But why take the southern route, the route that leads abroad, when in the east are provinces which need this natural gas, demand it and stand ready to buy it?
Nothing is more natural than to insist that our natural resources be developed in Canada for the benefit of the people of Canada! Let Alberta first take advantage of her natural resources, but let her think afterwards of her sister provinces, before worrying about the needs abroad.
Have you ever considered the ridiculous situation in which Quebec and Ontario might find themselves should they have to import natural gas from the United States, while Alberta was exporting gas to our neighbours? For heaven's sake, let us act more consistently and, above all, show more patriotism.
If Canada had a surplus of gas available, it would be a different matter altogether. If, for instance, Quebec and Ontario could be supplied natural gas without going to Alberta,

we would no doubt advise our friends in Calgary to sell some to the United States and we would then consider it our duty to help them to do so.
Exports are justified and can be profitable under two conditions. First, there must be a surplus available of the product that we want to export. But just the opposite is taking place. Supplies are insufficient. Secondly, the export of a product may be justified when supplies of it are sufficiently ample to satisfy local needs even though for financial reasons it has been decided to do without it in order to reap benefits from its sale. We have seen Great Britain for instance, and other European countries, selling us wares which had disappeared from their shops. The financial position of Great Britain was such that its citizens had to do without these products which were sent abroad in order to bring back precious dollars. That is not at all our case just now. Our financial situation does not require that we make such a sacrifice. What sacrifices there are must be made by the taxpayers of this country who deprive themselves in order to meet their tax payments.
Nothing then can justify the export of natural gas to the United States. On the contrary there is every necessity for Alberta satisfying as quickly as possible the requirements of the people of Canada.
Often in the past we have complained of having had to import the products we were badly in need of.
We have naturally complained that the exporter would set his own prices, if he were in a position to do so, because very often we could not get the kind of service we would have liked to receive. We are now in a position to obtain our natural gas at home, in Canada, but instead of supplying our own needs we are going to exhaust our resources by exporting that product to another country, namely the United States.
My hon. friend from Three Rivers gave evidence the other day to the effect that the government of the province of Quebec, as well as that of Ontario, wished to foster the building of a pipe line across Canada, and that neither of these provinces wished to import natural gas from Texas or elsewhere, while a Canadian province could easily supply that product. In that connection, the member for Three Rivers quoted a statement by the premier of the province of Quebec and

another by the minister of mines for Ontario. The statements of those two gentlemen cannot be taken lightly.

speechtext: They need to be enlightened.

You give me proof that we should keep our natural gas at home.
It would be unthinkable that the governments of Quebec and Ontario should now learn that Alberta, which they tried to encourage on grounds of patriotism and national unity, as I have stated a while ago, has now reversed her policy and decided to sell her products to people outside our own country.
Under such circumstances, there would be no cause to be surprised should the stand taken by Calgary be denounced both in Toronto and Quebec, and should Alberta feel that she were more or less being left aside.
Can our confederation stand such disunity? I do not think so. All parties interested should examine this problem calmly and from every angle and I am sure that they will then come to the same conclusion. The project may, at first sight, offer certain advantages, but they are negligible compared with the disadvantages that would ensue.
A country can only prosper in an atmosphere of harmony and mutual understanding. Such harmony and mutual understanding sometimes imply certain sacrifices on both sides-it is everyone's lot, now and then- but they are worth while.
We all want to see Canada keep on progressing, to see our natural resources add more and more to our national wealth and raise still further our standard of living. However, we might very well jeopardize this promising future if, instead of acting as a team, as shareholders in the same company, our sole concern is to please people abroad. Let us think first of ourselves and our own people; nobody can expect more.
I therefore believe, Mr. Speaker, that in the name of national unity, of national harmony, as well as in the name of our economic interests we must, without hesitation, reject [DOT]this request which is made to us.
The Progressive Conservative party has always championed private enterprise and it still does to this day. It will nevertheless never allow private enterprise to work against the national interest. There is no better way of ensuring the future of this country. There is no better way either of ensuring the future of private enterprise in Canada.

In that article the august journal said that the House of Commons was making a spectacle of itself. Of course it is the prerogative of those who sit outside in ivory towers to prejudge and so declare; but I think it was Bobbie Burns who said:'
O wad some power the giftie gie us To see oursels as ithers see us!
The Financial Post went on to say that the House of Commons was delaying most important business. That, of course, suggested some of the superiority complex which affects editorial writers when they presume to write about matters upon which they are not too well informed; because the editorial writer did not realize that this hour is provided for private members and, no matter how these private members' matters are discussed, they do not interfere with the business of Canada.
